excerpt: How machines find each other by name: the address behind every name, why a page loads when a number will not, and how device names help you read your own network.

body.text: This lesson explains how machines find each other by name. You will learn what an address does, why names exist at all, and how the names in your router's device list help you spot a stranger.
Every device on a network has a number called an address. Names exist because people remember words better than long strings of digits, and a name service translates one into the other.
Before you start

items: About twenty minutes.
The router's settings page, if you can reach it.
A notebook for two addresses.

body.text: Two kinds of name

items: A domain name is the word you type, such as a bank's website.
The name service turns that word into a number the network can route.
An address is the number, and it can change when the provider reassigns it.
A device name is what your own machine calls itself, such as Acer-Laptop.
An address on the home network is private, and only the house uses it.
The public address is the one the world sees, and the router holds it.

body.text: The router's device list will show a name beside each address, and many of the names will be cryptic strings from the factory. Those strings are normal, since manufacturers set them before the phone ever reaches a shop.

body.alt: A paper telephone directory beside a smartphone.
body.caption: A name and a number, in two places at once. The network does the same lookup thousands of times an hour.

body.text: It looks like a name and an address are the same thing. They are two records of one machine, and either can be wrong while the other is correct.
Why a name fails and a number works
When a page will not open, the name lookup is often the part that fails. The line is fine, and the name cannot be resolved.

items: Test one page by its address if you know it, which skips the lookup.
Restart the router, which clears a stale lookup table.
Change the name service in the router's settings to a public one.
Check the date and time on the device, since a wrong clock breaks secure lookups.
Try the same page on another device, which tells you whether the fault is local.
Report it only after the other steps, since a name fault looks like a dead line.

body.text: A browser will show a message about the server's address not being found, and the page will stay blank while other sites open. That message is about the lookup rather than the connection.

body.alt: A small network switch with several cables plugged in.
body.caption: A switch passes traffic by address. Names are handled elsewhere, which is why one can fail while the other works.

body.text: Reading your own device list

items: Open the router's page and find the list of attached devices.
Count them, and compare with the number of devices you own.
Rename your own devices so the list becomes readable.
Look for a device that is attached and unfamiliar.
Change the wifi password if a device does not belong.
Reconnect your own devices one by one afterwards.

body.text: The list will open with a column of addresses and a column of names, and a count at the top. Reading it once a month is enough to catch a device that should not be there.
Do not worry about the factory names looking strange. Renaming your own devices takes five minutes and makes the list useful from then on.
If it goes wrong
Every case here has a plain cause, and none of them needs a technician.

items: One site fails and others open: that site's name record is broken, so try again later.
Every site fails: the lookup is down, so restart the router and check the clock.
A device has two addresses: one is old and has not expired yet.
A name you renamed has changed back: the device renewed its old name on reconnecting.
The router page will not open: check the address printed on its label.
A stranger appears in the list: change the password and reconnect your own devices.

body.text: Practice
Make your own list readable.

items: Open the router's device list.
Count the devices and compare with your own.
Rename two devices with names you recognise.
Write the private address of one device in your notebook.
Repeat the count in a month.

body.text: You can now read a network by its names. In the next lesson you will share a printer and a folder across an office.

excerpt: Sharing a printer and a folder at work without exposing everything: what to share, who should reach it, and how to take access away again.

body.text: This lesson shows you how to share a printer and a folder across a small office. You will learn what to share, who should be able to open it, and how to remove access when somebody leaves.
Sharing is a permission rather than a copy. The file stays on one machine, and other machines are allowed to read it, which is why a wrong setting can expose more than you meant.
Before you start

items: Two machines on the same network.
The printer, and its driver if you have it.
About thirty minutes.

body.text: Sharing a printer

items: Connect the printer to one machine and install its driver there.
Open the printer settings on that machine and turn on sharing.
Give the shared printer a clear name, such as FrontDesk-HP.
On the second machine, add a printer and choose the network option.
Select the shared printer and let it install.
Print one test page and keep it as proof that the setup works.

body.text: The printer list will show the shared name under a network heading, and the second machine will treat it as its own. A test page from the far machine is the only proof worth having.

body.alt: A shared office printer beside a desk.
body.caption: One printer, several machines. Sharing works until the host machine sleeps, which is the usual complaint.

body.text: It looks like a shared printer needs its own network cable. Most small offices share one attached to a single machine, and that machine must stay awake.
Sharing a folder

items: Create a folder named for its purpose, not for a person.
Right-click and open the sharing settings.
Choose the people who may open it, and give them read access first.
Add write access only to the people who must change files.
Send the network path, which looks like two backslashes and a name.
Test it from the second machine before telling anybody else.

body.text: The folder window will show a small icon of two people once it is shared, and the permissions box will list each name with a level beside it. If the list is empty, nobody else can open it.

body.alt: Two laptops on one office desk connected to the same network.
body.caption: Two machines, one folder. Read access for most people, write access for the few who need it.

body.text: A permissions box will show read and write as separate choices. Giving both to everybody is the mistake that turns a shared folder into a place where files disappear.
What not to share

items: A whole drive, since one mistake exposes every folder on it.
Payroll, medical, or identity documents on a shared folder.
A folder on a personal machine that leaves the office.
Guest access without a password.
Anything with a name that tells a stranger what is inside.
Write access for people who only need to read.

body.text: None of this needs a server. A folder, a short list of names, and two levels of access cover most small offices.
Do not worry about getting it wrong on the first try. Access can be removed at any time, and removing it is the part most people never practise.
If it goes wrong
Every case here has a setting behind it, and each one is fixable.

items: The printer disappears: the host machine went to sleep or restarted.
The folder asks for a password: the guest account is off, which is safer.
Files vanish from the folder: somebody with write access moved them.
The second machine cannot see the share: the two are on different networks.
A former staff member still opens it: remove the name, then change the password.
Printing is slow: the host machine is busy, and a direct network printer is faster.

body.text: Practice
Build one small share and check it from the other side.

items: Create a folder called Shared-Documents.
Share it with read access for two people.
Open it from the second machine using the network path.
Try to delete a file there and watch the refusal.
Remove one name and confirm that person can no longer open it.

body.text: You can now share without exposing everything. In the next lesson you will deal with the neighbours on your wifi.

excerpt: When the signal reaches the next building: how neighbours end up on your network, what a guest network does, and how to take access back politely.

body.text: This lesson is about the neighbours and your wifi. You will learn how a signal reaches the next building, why a shared password becomes a habit, and how to take access back without a quarrel.
Radio does not stop at a wall. A router in a compound with thin walls can serve three buildings, and a password given once is rarely taken back.
Before you start

items: Access to the router's settings page.
A count of the devices you actually own.
About twenty minutes.

body.text: How it happens

items: Somebody asks for the password to check one message.
The phone remembers the network and reconnects every day.
The password is passed to a cousin, who passes it on.
A repeater in the next building extends the same network.
Nobody notices until the evenings become slow.
The list of attached devices is the only record.

body.text: The router's device list will show a dozen names, and most will be factory strings rather than people. Counting them against the devices in your own house is the first honest measure.

body.alt: A notebook with a written password beside a router.
body.caption: A password written down and passed around. A guest network keeps that habit away from your own devices.

body.text: It looks like sharing a password is only a kindness. It is also a small loan of your line, your speed, and your risk, and loans are easier to give than to recall.
The guest network
Most routers can run a second network for visitors, separate from yours.

items: Open the router's settings and find the guest network option.
Give it a name that does not identify your house.
Set a password you are willing to change monthly.
Turn off access to your own devices from the guest network.
Set the guest network to switch off at night if the router allows it.
Write the guest password somewhere you can find it again.

body.text: The settings page will show the guest network as a second row with its own name and password. Keeping the two rows separate is the whole point, since a guest never needs to reach your laptop.

body.alt: A wall between neighbouring buildings with a view of rooftops.
body.caption: A wall stops people, not radio. Distance and a second network do more than a fence.

body.text: Taking access back

items: Change the main wifi password, which disconnects everybody at once.
Reconnect your own devices one by one.
Tell the neighbours the guest password instead, if you want to keep helping.
Move the router away from the shared wall.
Lower the transmit power if the router offers it.
Check the device list again in a week.

body.text: A new password will appear in the router's page at once, and every device will ask for it again. That inconvenience is the evidence that the old password has stopped working.
Do not worry about the conversation. Offering the guest network gives a neighbour a way to stay connected without giving them your own line.
If it goes wrong
Every case here has a way back, and none of them needs a new router.

items: Your own devices will not reconnect: the password was typed with a capital or a space.
The guest network cannot print: that is the separation working as intended.
Speed drops in the evening: count the devices before blaming the provider.
A neighbour is upset: offer the guest password and a limit on heavy use.
The signal still reaches next door: lower the power or move the router inward.
Somebody changed the router password: reset the router and set it up again.

body.text: Practice
Separate the two networks this week.

items: Count the devices attached to your network.
Turn on the guest network with its own password.
Change the main password and reconnect your own devices.
Tell one neighbour the guest password.
Count again in a week and compare.

body.text: You can now keep your line for your own house. In the next lesson you will use a phone as a rescue wire when the line fails.

excerpt: Using a phone as a hotspot or a USB modem: what it costs, how to set it up, and how to keep the battery and the bundle alive.

body.text: This lesson shows you how to use a phone as a rescue wire. You will learn the difference between a hotspot and a cable, how to set either up in a minute, and how to keep the bundle from disappearing.
A phone with data is a small router. Sharing that data is called tethering, and it is the reason a working phone can carry an office through an outage.
Before you start

items: A phone with data and a charged battery.
A USB cable, if you want the steadier option.
About fifteen minutes.

body.text: Two ways to share

items: A hotspot sends wifi from the phone, and several devices can join.
A USB cable shares the connection with one machine and charges the phone.
Bluetooth sharing works, though it is slower than either.
A hotspot drains the battery quickly, so keep the phone plugged in.
A cable is steadier for a video call, since it does not drop.
Both use the same bundle, which is the part people forget.

body.text: You will see a new wifi name appear in the laptop's list, named after the phone. Joining it takes the password shown on the phone's hotspot screen, which you can change to something you will remember.

body.alt: A laptop connected to a phone's wifi hotspot on a desk.
body.caption: A phone, a laptop, and a bundle. The hotspot is a router that fits in a pocket and bills by the megabyte.

body.text: It looks like tethering is free because the phone already has data. The data is the same bundle, and a laptop uses it faster than a phone ever does.
Setting up a hotspot

items: Open settings and find the hotspot or tethering option.
Set a name that does not include your full name.
Set a password of at least eight characters.
Turn on the hotspot and join it from the laptop.
Set a data limit in the phone's settings if it offers one.
Turn the hotspot off when you finish, since it stays on otherwise.

body.text: The hotspot screen will show how many devices are connected and how much data has passed. That figure is the check to watch, since a connected device keeps using data in the background.

body.alt: A phone connected to a laptop by a USB cable for tethering.
body.caption: The cable option. One machine, no password, and the phone charges while it works.

body.text: The laptop will show a cable connection instead of a wifi one when tethering by USB. There is no password to type, and the phone gains charge rather than losing it.
Keeping the bundle alive

items: Turn off automatic updates on the laptop before connecting.
Close cloud sync for photographs and large folders.
Set the laptop to use less data for video calls.
Watch the phone's data counter during the session.
Disconnect when the urgent task is done.
Keep a small bundle for rescue only, separate from the daily one.

body.text: None of this needs a special plan. Two settings, updates and cloud sync, are the difference between a rescue and a bill.
Do not worry about the setup taking long. Once the hotspot name and password are set, a rescue takes under a minute.
If it goes wrong
Every case here has a cause, and most are settings rather than hardware.

items: The laptop cannot find the hotspot: the hotspot band may be set to the newer one only.
The hotspot keeps dropping: the phone is saving power, so keep the screen awake.
The bundle finishes in a day: an update or a sync ran in the background.
USB tethering does nothing: the cable carries power only, so try another cable.
The phone becomes hot: a hotspot uses the radio hard, so let it cool and plug it in.
The carrier blocks tethering: check the plan's terms before relying on it.

body.text: Practice
Test the rescue before you need it.

items: Set the hotspot name and password.
Note the phone's data counter before connecting.
Connect the laptop, load one page, then disconnect.
Note the counter again, and see what a page cost.
Repeat with a USB cable and compare the steadiness.

body.text: You can now keep working when the line fails. In the next lesson you will build a small network for a shop.

excerpt: A network sized for a counter: the till, the phone, the customer wifi, and the power plan that keeps them running through an outage.

body.text: This lesson builds a small network for a small shop. You will learn what to connect, how to keep customers off the till's network, and how to plan for power that fails.
A shop needs less than an office and more than a home. Two networks, one router, and a way to keep the till working through a power cut cover most counters.
Before you start

items: The till or POS terminal, and the phone used for transfers.
The router, and its power adapter.
About one hour.

body.text: What belongs on the network

items: The till or POS terminal, on a network of its own.
The shop phone, on the same network as the till.
The camera system, if there is one, on the till's network.
Customer wifi, on a guest network with its own password.
A backup phone with data, kept charged.
Nothing personal, since a shop machine is shared by staff.

body.text: You decide this list once, and everything else follows from it. If you can name what belongs on the till's network, you can tell what does not, and that is the judgement a shop needs.
The router's page will show two rows when the guest network is on, one for the shop and one for customers. Keeping them apart is the setting that protects the till.

On the counter phone, the wifi list will show two shop networks, one for the till and one for customers, and you can see at a glance which one you are joined to. Join the shop network yourself when you need to check the terminal.

body.alt: A small shop counter with a computer and card machine.
body.caption: The counter is the network's centre. The till, the phone, and the camera belong together.

body.text: It looks like customer wifi is a kindness with no cost. On one shared network, a customer's infected phone sits beside the till, and the guest network costs nothing to switch on.
Power, which is the real problem
A network that dies with the light is not a network. Plan the power before the cabling.

items: Put the router on a small uninterruptible supply or an inverter circuit.
Keep the till on the same supply as the router.
Charge the backup phone every evening, not when it dies.
Keep a power bank for the POS terminal if it has no battery.
Protect the supply from surges with a good extension and a surge guard.
Test the setup by switching off the mains for five minutes.

body.text: The router's lights will stay on during a test cut, and the till will keep its connection. If either dies, the supply is the thing to fix rather than the network.

body.alt: A small network hub on a shop shelf with cables.
body.caption: A hub on a shelf, out of the way and above the floor. Dust and feet break more shop networks than providers do.

body.text: Layout and habits

items: Put the router high, near the counter, away from the safe and the metal shelving.
Run cables along the wall rather than across the floor.
Label each cable at both ends.
Change the customer password monthly and post it at the counter.
Turn the customer network off after closing.
Write the provider's number and the router's password in the shop book.

body.text: Before you buy anything, write down what you will connect and where the power will come from. You will find that the list is short, and that the power plan matters more than the router.
None of this needs a technician on call. Two networks, one supply, and one notebook cover a shop of this size.
Do not worry about the cost of the supply. A small unit costs less than one lost evening of card payments.
If it goes wrong
Every case here is a shop-sized problem with a shop-sized fix.

items: The till loses connection at the same hour: a staff phone is syncing on the same network.
Card payments fail and transfers work: the terminal's provider is down, not your line.
The camera drops when the router restarts: reconnect it, and give it a fixed address.
Customers cannot join the wifi: the password changed and the sign is old.
The router dies in a power cut: the supply is too small for the load.
Speed is slow with one customer connected: the guest network shares the same line.

body.text: Practice
Run the shop's first test cut.

items: Switch on the guest network with its own password.
Move the router and the till onto the backup supply.
Switch off the mains for five minutes and watch the lights.
Take one card payment while the mains is off.
Write the result in the shop book.

body.text: You can now keep a counter online through a bad evening. The next chapter looks at the technician's habits, starting with listening.
